title: The Maximal Function and Lebesgue Differentiation

items.title: A locally integrable function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: Define $L^1_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ through integrability on every Euclidean ball, keeping both measurability and finite ball integral requirements explicit because later averages are taken over balls and not over arbitrary compact sets.

items.title: Euclidean balls have positive finite Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: Sandwich a Euclidean ball between two axis-parallel boxes of comparable side lengths. The box-measure theorem then gives both positivity and finiteness, which is the only denominator control the averaging definitions need.

items.title: The average of a locally integrable function over a Euclidean ball
items.strategy: Fix the page notation $A_r f(x)$ as the normalized integral over $B(x,r)$, citing the preceding ball-measure lemma so the denominator is already known to be finite and nonzero.

items.title: The centered and uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal functions
items.strategy: Define the centered maximal function through the ball averages and the uncentered maximal function through all balls containing the point. Keeping both objects visible now makes the later comparison theorem honest instead of folding one convention into the other silently.

items.title: Sublinear operators and weak or strong type $(p,q)$ bounds
items.strategy: Record the exact language used by Marcinkiewicz interpolation: sublinearity, strong type, and weak type written through superlevel-set estimates. The page only needs the diagonal cases, but the definition should state the general $(p,q)$ form once.

items.title: Lebesgue points and the Lebesgue set of an $L^1_{loc}$ class
items.strategy: Define the Lebesgue-point condition through the averaged absolute oscillation and state the Lebesgue set at the level of the $L^1_{loc}$ class, because later examples use representatives that differ on null sets.

items.title: Density of a measurable set at a point
items.strategy: Define density through the normalized ball measures and keep the target values $0$ and $1$ separate from the definition, so the later density theorem remains a theorem rather than being hidden in the vocabulary.

items.title: A family shrinking nicely to a point
items.strategy: Use the standard containment and comparable-measure condition: $E_r \subseteq B(x,r)$ and $\lambda(E_r)$ dominates a fixed fraction of $\lambda(B(x,r))$. The eccentricity constant has to be part of the data because later theorems quote it explicitly.

items.title: Vitali covering lemma for Euclidean balls with fivefold dilates
items.strategy: First prove the finite greedy-selection lemma: choose balls in decreasing-radius order, note every discarded ball meets a chosen one of at least the same radius, and use the triangle inequality to get fivefold coverage. Then state the countable bounded-radius form by the same greedy recursion, marking the countable-choice cost explicitly.

items.title: Ball averages vary continuously with the centre and radius
items.strategy: Write the average as the integral of $f$ against the ball indicator divided by the ball measure. Away from the boundary sphere the indicators converge pointwise, and dominated convergence handles the numerator; the denominator is continuous because balls scale by a fixed positive volume factor.

items.title: The centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is Borel measurable
items.strategy: Prove that each superlevel set $\{Mf>t\}$ is open: if one average at $x$ exceeds $t$, continuity of the average in the centre preserves that inequality on a neighbourhood. This is the load-bearing topological step the design singled out.

items.title: The centered and uncentered maximal functions are pointwise comparable
items.strategy: Any centered ball is also an uncentered ball, giving $M \le M^*$. Conversely, if $x$ lies in a ball $B(y,r)$, then $B(y,r) \subseteq B(x,2r)$, so the volume ratio bounds the uncentered average by $2^n$ times the centered one.

items.title: The centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is weak type $(1,1)$
items.strategy: For a compact subset of the superlevel set, choose one witnessing ball at each point, pass to a finite subcover, apply the Vitali ball lemma, and bound the measure of the compact set by the sum of the disjoint ball integrals. State the resulting estimate with the design’s honest $5^n$ constant rather than claiming sharpness.

items.title: The centered maximal operator is bounded on $L^\infty$
items.strategy: Every normalized ball average of $|f|$ is bounded by the essential supremum of $f$, so taking the supremum over radii does not enlarge the bound.

items.title: Marcinkiewicz interpolation from weak $(1,1)$ and strong $(\infty,\infty)$
items.strategy: Use the real-variable truncation argument the design chose: split $f$ at height $t/2$, control the high part by the weak $(1,1)$ estimate, the low part by the $L^\infty$ estimate, and integrate the distribution-function bound with the layer-cake formula. Keep the operator sublinear throughout so the proof applies to maximal operators.

items.title: The centered maximal operator is bounded on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $1<p<\infty$
items.strategy: Apply the Marcinkiewicz theorem to the centered maximal operator using the weak $(1,1)$ bound and the $L^\infty$ bound already proved on this page. The uncentered estimate then follows immediately from the comparison proposition.

items.title: Riesz-Thorin interpolation theorem
items.strategy: Reduce first to finite simple functions on finite-measure supports, pair $Tf$ against a finite simple test function, and build the strip function whose boundary bounds encode the endpoint operator norms. The proof contains its own three-lines argument in the special strip form needed here, so no later complex-analysis theorem is imported.

items.title: Continuous compactly supported functions are recovered by small ball averages
items.strategy: Use continuity at the centre point: once $g$ varies by at most $\varepsilon$ on a sufficiently small ball, the normalized average differs from $g(x)$ by at most $\varepsilon$. This is the dense-subclass step of the differentiation proof and deserves its own item.

items.title: Lebesgue differentiation theorem on $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: Follow the standard three-step route named in the design: prove the statement for continuous compactly supported functions, approximate the general function in $L^1$ on a large ball by such a function using MT-15 density, and control the bad set for the error term with the maximal inequality and Chebyshev-Markov.

items.title: Almost every point is a Lebesgue point of a locally integrable function
items.strategy: Apply the differentiation theorem to $|f-c|$ for each rational real or Gaussian rational complex constant $c$, take the union of the resulting null sets, and use the density of those constants to pass from convergence of averages of $|f-c|$ to convergence of the averaged oscillation. The one-null-set quantifier order is the whole point.

items.title: Lebesgue density theorem
items.strategy: Apply the Lebesgue-point theorem to the indicator of a measurable set. At points of the Lebesgue set the average oscillation of the indicator forces the density to be $1$ on the set and $0$ on its complement.

items.title: Differentiation holds along families shrinking nicely
items.strategy: Compare the average over each shrinking family with the average over its containing ball. The lower measure bound in the definition of shrinking nicely turns the Lebesgue-point estimate over balls into the same estimate for the family.

items.title: Differentiation of sigma-finite Borel measures finite on compact sets
items.strategy: Write the given measure as $\nu = f\,d\lambda + \nu_s$ using the Lebesgue decomposition and Radon-Nikodym density from MT-13. The absolutely continuous part is handled by the shrinking-family differentiation theorem applied to $f$, and the singular part is shown to contribute zero almost everywhere by the same relative-density argument used in the classical measure-differentiation theorem.

items.title: The indefinite integral of an $L^1$ function is differentiable almost everywhere
items.strategy: Extend $f\in L^1[a,b]$ by zero outside the interval and rewrite the difference quotient of $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ as the average of that extension over the one-sided interval family $[x,x+h]$. Those intervals shrink nicely to $x$, so the differentiation theorem supplies the almost-everywhere derivative formula.

items.title: The Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is not strong type $(1,1)$
items.strategy: For a nonzero $f\in L^1$, choose a measurable set of positive finite measure on which $|f|$ is bounded below by a positive constant. Every sufficiently distant point is the centre of a large ball containing that set, which forces $Mf(x) \gtrsim |x|^{-n}$; that tail is not integrable on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

title: The Maximal Function and Lebesgue Differentiation — Examples

items.title: The centered maximal function of $\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}$ on $\mathbb{R}$
items.strategy: Compute the maximizing interval explicitly. Inside $[0,1]$ the maximal average is $1$; to the right it is attained by the shortest centered interval that reaches $0$, and to the left by the shortest centered interval that reaches $1$, producing the reciprocal tail.

items.title: The maximal function of $\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}$ is not integrable
items.strategy: Use the closed-form computation from the preceding example: the tail equals $1/(2x)$ for $x\ge1$, so the integral of the maximal function over $[1,\infty)$ diverges logarithmically.

items.title: A unit-mass spike has a large maximal superlevel set
items.strategy: Take $f_\varepsilon = \varepsilon^{-1}\mathbf{1}_{[0,\varepsilon]}$. For $x \ge \varepsilon$, the centered interval of radius $x$ already contains the support and gives $Mf_\varepsilon(x) \ge (2x)^{-1}$, which makes the weak-type scaling visible on one concrete family.

items.title: The $L^1_{loc}$ class of $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ has every point as a Lebesgue point
items.strategy: Use that $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}=0$ almost everywhere, so the class in $L^1_{loc}$ is the zero class. The zero class has the whole line as its Lebesgue set, which is the cleanest witness that the page works at the class level.

items.title: An endpoint of an interval has density one half, not one
items.strategy: At an interior point of an interval the density is $1$, but at an endpoint the symmetric ball sees exactly half the interval and half the complement. This gives the cheapest concrete point of a measurable set that is not a density point.

items.title: A positive-measure compact set can miss part of every interval
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in $(0,1)$ and cover the $k$th rational by an interval of length at most $2^{-k-3}$; their union is open, dense, and has measure below $1/2$. Its complement in $[0,1]$ is compact by Heine--Borel and has positive measure by subadditivity, while density of the removed union ensures that the compact set never fills an interval completely.

items.title: Steinhaus follows in two lines from the density theorem
items.strategy: Choose a density point $x$ of a positive-measure set $E$ and a small ball on which $E$ fills more than half the measure. Small translates of that ball still overlap it in positive measure, so some point belongs to both $E$ and its translate, which puts the translation vector in $E-E$.

items.title: FALSE: some measurable set has density one half in every interval
items.strategy: If such a set had measure zero, the unit interval would already contradict the claimed half-density. If it had positive measure, then the density theorem would force density $1$ at almost every point of the set, contradicting the universal density-$1/2$ requirement.

items.title: A locally integrable function can fail to differentiate on a null set
items.strategy: Use the alternating dyadic-annulus indicator $f=\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbf{1}_{(2^{-2k-1},2^{-2k})}$. It is bounded and locally integrable, but the centered averages at $0$ along radii $2^{-2m}$ and $2^{-2m-1}$ approach two different values, so the differentiation limit fails on the singleton null set $\{0\}$.
